lessons.title: What Is Money?
lessons.keyIdea: Money isn't defined by what it's made of — it's defined by what it does.

blocks.text: For most of human history — over 6,000 years — barter was how people exchanged what they had for what they needed: trading goods or services directly, with no money involved. It worked, but it had one serious flaw.

Both people in a trade have to want exactly what the other one has, at the same time. A farmer with vegetables who wants shoes has to find a shoemaker who happens to want vegetables — not meat, not tools. If not, the trade just doesn't happen.

blocks.text: As trade grew, that stopped scaling. What was needed was something everyone would accept, regardless of what they personally wanted that day — which is exactly what money is. To count as real money, something generally has to do three things at once:

A medium of exchange (widely accepted in trade), a store of value (holds its worth over time so you can save it), and a unit of account (a common measure for comparing the value of very different things — how many chickens is a cow worth?).

Gold became the dominant choice almost everywhere it was available — scarce, durable, divisible, and easy to verify. The first standardized gold and silver coins date to the Kingdom of Lydia, around 700 B.C. But because money is defined by function and not material, gold was never the only option.

In prisoner-of-war camps during the Second World War, cigarettes functioned as real, working currency — divisible, portable, and valued by everyone (even non-smokers) because everyone knew everyone else would accept them. Prices were quoted "in cigarettes," debts were tracked in cigarettes, and the camp's money supply rose and fell with Red Cross parcel deliveries. This is a real, documented case (R.A. Radford's 1945 account of a WWII POW camp economy) — and it's the cleanest proof that money is about trust and function, not what it's made of.

It's tempting to think a currency's value is fixed or "real," the way a gold coin feels real. It isn't. Every currency's value — including the ones you'll see priced elsewhere in this app — is a reflection of collective trust and expectation. That's precisely why currency values move, and why markets like this one exist at all.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three functions of money?
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account are the three real functions. "Store of physical weight" isn't one of them.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — re-read the three functions: medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account.

quiz.question: True or False: money must be a physical object made of something valuable, like gold, to function as money.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — money is defined by function, not material. Cigarettes in a WWII POW camp worked as real money.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — remember the POW camp example. Money just needs trust and acceptance, not physical value.

Both people in a trade must want exactly what the other has, at the same time.
Something widely accepted in trade for goods and services.
Something that holds its purchasing power over time.
A common measure for comparing the value of different things.
Limited supply — a key trait that let gold hold value as money.

lessons.title: Gold's Problems and the Birth of Paper Money
lessons.keyIdea: Gold solved barter — but its own weight and fixed supply created problems that paper money was invented to fix.

blocks.text: Gold was excellent as money for a long time — but as trade grew larger and more complex, it ran into four real problems: it could be secretly debased, its value could shift when new gold was discovered, it was heavy and risky to transport, and there was often not enough of it in circulation to match the pace of trade.
Secretly reducing the amount of precious metal in a coin — mixing in cheaper metal — while still presenting it as full value.
The core fix was simple: instead of physically carrying gold everywhere, leave it with someone trustworthy for safekeeping, and trade the paper receipt instead.

A paper document promising the holder can redeem it for a real asset — in this case gold — on demand. Merchant receipts like this existed in China as early as the 7th century; goldsmiths in 17th-century England ran a very similar system.

This solved gold's transport problem — but created a new one. Once many goldsmiths and banks were each issuing their own paper notes, a note from one issuer often wasn't trusted or accepted far from where it came from.

A banking system where a bank holds only a fraction of the deposits it's responsible for in actual reserve, and lends out — or issues notes against — the rest. It's genuinely useful (it's how banks fund loans and business investment) but it comes with a structural risk.

blocks.text: A situation where many depositors try to withdraw their funds at once, faster than the bank can pay out, because it only holds a fraction of deposits in reserve.

A bank holds 100 gold coins but has issued 500 IOU notes against them. On an ordinary day this works fine — only a few people ever ask for their gold at once. But if confidence drops and everyone tries to redeem on the same day, the bank runs out of gold long before it runs out of notes to honor. The panic itself becomes the crisis.

To fix both problems — too many competing currencies, and the instability of fractional reserve banking — countries began establishing central banks. The Bank of England, founded in 1694, is one of the earliest examples: a single, trusted institution issuing one national currency and regulating the banks around it.

The same tension keeps showing up: a disciplined system builds trust, but that discipline can be too rigid in a crisis. You'll see this exact trade-off again with the gold standard itself in the next lesson.

quiz.question: What does fractional reserve banking actually allow a bank to do?
options: Hold more gold than it lends out
Lend out or issue notes for more than it holds in reserve
Print unlimited paper money with no risk
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — that's exactly what fractional reserve banking is: holding only a fraction of deposits, and lending or issuing notes against the rest.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — re-read the definition: a bank holds only a fraction of deposits in reserve, and lends out the rest.

quiz.question: True or False: a bank run happens because the bank did something wrong that specific day.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a bank run is a confidence problem, not necessarily a wrongdoing problem. The bank can be doing exactly what it always does and still run out if enough people show up at once.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — a bank run can happen even when the bank hasn't changed anything. It's about many people demanding withdrawal at the same time, not a specific mistake that day.

keyTerms.def: Secretly reducing the precious-metal content of a coin.
A paper promise redeemable for a real asset on demand.
Holding only part of deposits in reserve, lending out the rest.
Many depositors demanding withdrawal at once, faster than the bank can pay.
The official institution that issues a country's currency and regulates its banks.

lessons.title: The Rise and Fall of the Gold Standard
lessons.keyIdea: A fixed, disciplined system prevents abuse — but that same rigidity leaves no room to maneuver when a real crisis hits.

blocks.text: The United States formally adopted the gold standard in 1879 — every dollar in circulation became directly redeemable for a fixed amount of gold, for ordinary citizens, not just foreign governments. Britain had done the same decades earlier, in 1821.
A monetary system in which a currency is directly backed by, and freely convertible into, a fixed quantity of gold.

It worked — until a war forced every participating country to choose between keeping its promise to gold and paying for the war. When World War I began in 1914, major economies suspended gold convertibility so they could print the money needed to fund it.

Britain rejoined the gold standard in 1925, at the same rate the pound held before the war — a decision that overvalued the pound relative to Britain's actual post-war economic strength, and strained its economy for years.

An interwar variant of the gold standard in which some countries held actual gold reserves, while others held reserves of a gold-convertible currency (like the British pound) instead of gold itself — more fragile than the pre-war original.

blocks.text: When the Great Depression hit in 1929, countries still on the gold standard faced an impossible choice: defending a fixed gold peg meant keeping interest rates high and the money supply tight — the opposite of what a struggling economy needs to recover.
The actions a central bank takes to manage a country's money supply and interest rates, typically to influence inflation, employment, and growth.
A general decline in prices across an economy over time — the opposite of inflation — which can deepen a recession by encouraging people to delay spending.

In 1933, with U.S. gold reserves under severe strain, the government required citizens to exchange gold coin and bullion for currency, ending public redemption of dollars for gold domestically. In 1934, the Gold Reserve Act officially devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35 per ounce — the U.S. left the domestic gold standard, but kept a modified, international-only version alive at that new rate.
A deliberate reduction in a currency's official value, typically relative to another asset or currency.
That $35-per-ounce rate is not a random number — it is exactly the rate Bretton Woods would formalize internationally ten years later, in 1944. Keep it in mind for the next lesson.

quiz.question: Why did Britain's 1925 return to the gold standard strain its economy?
options: Gold had become too cheap to be useful
It rejoined at an overvalued pre-war exchange rate
It printed far too much money that year
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — rejoining at the old pre-war rate overvalued the pound relative to the real post-war economy, straining it for years.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — the issue was the exchange rate Britain rejoined at, not the money supply or a ban on gold.

quiz.question: True or False: a strict gold standard makes it easier for a government to fight a recession.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a strict gold standard actually makes it harder, since fighting a recession usually requires expanding the money supply beyond what gold reserves allow.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — it's the opposite. Defending a fixed gold peg during a recession usually means tightening money, not loosening it.

An interwar system mixing actual gold reserves with gold-convertible currency reserves.
Central bank actions managing money supply and interest rates.
A general decline in prices across an economy over time.
A deliberate reduction in a currency's official value.

lessons.title: Bretton Woods and the Birth of Forex
lessons.keyIdea: Forex exists because currencies float freely instead of being fixed to gold or to each other.

blocks.text: In July 1944, representatives of 44 Allied nations met in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design a new system: instead of every country backing its own currency with its own gold, every country would peg its currency to the U.S. dollar, and only the dollar would remain convertible to gold — at that same $35-per-ounce rate from 1934.
The 1944 international agreement under which most currencies were pegged to the U.S. dollar, while the dollar itself remained convertible to gold at a fixed rate.
A currency whose value is fixed, or held within a narrow band, relative to another currency rather than allowed to move freely.

blocks.text: This worked for a while — countries could hold U.S. dollars as reserves instead of physically shipping gold, making cross-border trade faster and cheaper. But a structural problem was building underneath it.

The conflict facing a country whose currency is the world's reserve currency: it must supply the world with enough of its currency for global trade, while keeping enough confidence in that currency to stay credible — two goals pulling in opposite directions.

To supply the world with dollars, the U.S. ran persistent deficits. But the more dollars circulated abroad, the harder it became to credibly promise every one could still convert to gold — especially as domestic inflation and war spending meant more dollars were printed than gold reserves could realistically back.

On August 15, 1971, President Nixon announced the U.S. would suspend the dollar's convertibility into gold — "closing the gold window." What was framed as temporary turned out to be permanent. A brief patch (the Smithsonian Agreement, December 1971) failed, and by 1973 major currencies had abandoned fixed pegs entirely.
The August 1971 announcement suspending the U.S. dollar's convertibility to gold, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system.
An exchange rate determined by open market supply and demand, rather than fixed or pegged by government agreement.
With the last tie between money and gold severed, the world entered the era of fiat currency — the system every major economy uses today.
Money that has value because a government declares it legal tender and people trust and accept it — not because it's backed by a physical commodity like gold.
A currency held in significant quantities by governments and institutions worldwide for trade and finance — the U.S. dollar has held this role since Bretton Woods.

This is the answer to the question this whole course has been building toward: forex exists specifically because currencies are no longer fixed to gold or each other. They float, they move — and where there's constant, unpredictable movement in something valuable, a market emerges to trade it. That market is the one you're learning to navigate.

quiz.question: What did the Nixon Shock actually announce?
options: The end of the dollar's convertibility to gold
A ban on foreign currency trading
The creation of a new reserve currency
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — Nixon announced the U.S. would suspend converting dollars into gold, which effectively ended Bretton Woods.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — it specifically ended dollar-to-gold convertibility, not trading itself or a new gold price.

quiz.question: True or False: floating exchange rates are the reason a forex market exists today.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — under fixed pegs there wasn't much to actively trade. Once rates floated freely after 1973, currency values became a live, moving target — which is exactly what created the modern forex market.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — this is actually true. Fixed exchange rates left little to trade; floating rates are what created the market.

keyTerms.def: The 1944 agreement pegging currencies to the U.S. dollar, itself pegged to gold.
A currency fixed in value relative to another currency.
The conflict facing a reserve-currency country between global liquidity and maintaining trust.
The 1971 suspension of the dollar's convertibility to gold.
An exchange rate set by open market supply and demand.
Money valuable because of government backing and trust, not a physical commodity.
A currency widely held by governments and institutions for global trade and finance.

lessons.title: What Is Risk, and How Do You Manage It?
lessons.keyIdea: Risk management is what makes a good trader — not the ability to predict market direction.

blocks.text: You are still not ready to place a trade. The single most important topic in this course is risk management. Skilled analysis without risk management doesn't produce a successful trader — it produces someone who is right sometimes and wiped out eventually.

Look at the job postings at any serious investment firm. You'll see plenty of listings for risk managers. You will not see a "profit-taking manager." These firms don't primarily focus on how much they're making — they focus on how much they could lose, and how to control it.
The possibility that an action or decision doesn't go the way you intended, exposing you to a loss or a bad outcome.

Risk isn't unique to trading — it's in everything. Skydiving carries risk. Flying to a vacation destination carries risk. Driving to work carries risk. The actual skill isn't avoiding risk altogether — that's impossible. It's judging whether a given risk is worth taking, and controlling it wherever you can.

The practice of identifying a risk, deciding whether it's worth taking, and — if so — actively controlling how much that risk could cost you. This applies identically whether you're trading a currency, a stock, or a crypto asset.
Acknowledging a risk exists and choosing to take on the entire potential downside, with no limit. Never used deliberately in trading — it means being willing to lose everything on one position.
Recognizing a risk is too high relative to the benefit, and simply not taking the action. Example: skipping a major central bank announcement rather than holding a position through it.
Accepting a risk exists, but capping how much it can cost you. This is what a stop-loss does mechanically — and it's the technique you'll use the most, by far.
Paying someone else to take on your risk — like insurance, or options/hedging in trading. Comes at an ongoing cost that erodes returns if overused.

A trader who is right only 40% of the time can be consistently profitable, if every loss is small and controlled while winners are allowed to run. A trader who is right 90% of the time can still go broke, if a single uncontrolled loss is large enough to erase every gain before it. Being right often is not the same as trading well.

quiz.question: Which risk management technique do traders rely on most heavily to cap potential losses?
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — Risk Limitation is the technique behind a stop-loss: accepting a risk exists, but capping exactly how much it can cost you.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — re-read the definitions. The technique behind a stop-loss caps a known risk rather than avoiding or transferring it.

quiz.question: True or False: the best traders are the ones who predict market direction correctly most often.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — prediction accuracy alone doesn't determine success. A trader who controls losses well can be profitable even with a mediocre prediction record.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — a trader with an excellent prediction record can still fail without proper risk management. One large, uncontrolled loss can erase many small wins.

Choosing not to take an action because the risk outweighs the benefit.

lessons.title: Setting a Stop-Loss — Where and Why
lessons.keyIdea: A stop-loss you decide on after you're already losing money is not risk management — it's hope with a delay.

blocks.text: Risk limitation is the technique you'll use the most. This lesson makes it concrete: every time you enter a position, there are three prices to think through.
The price at which you actually open a position.
The price at which you plan to exit if the position moves in your favor.
The price at which you plan to exit if the position moves against you, capping your loss at a known, fixed amount.

Risk management is almost entirely about the stop-loss. Making "too much" profit is never a problem worth solving. Losing more than you planned to is the only outcome risk management exists to prevent.
A position that profits if the price goes up. You buy now, expecting to sell later at a higher price.

You buy USD/CAD near a support zone at 1.34, believing the price will rise. Your take-profit sits above your entry. Your stop-loss sits below your entry — near the support zone, where price would have real difficulty falling through if your read is correct. If price falls to your stop instead, you exit there and move on.
A position that profits if the price goes down. You're effectively selling now, expecting to buy back later at a lower price.

You believe a pair is about to fall, so you short at 1.36. Your take-profit sits below your entry. Your stop-loss sits above your entry — if price rises instead of falling, that proves you wrong, and you exit there.

blocks.text: A stop-loss you decide on after you're already losing money is not risk management — it's hope with a delay. The entire value of a stop-loss comes from setting it before you enter, while you're still thinking clearly.

quiz.question: You enter a long position on a currency pair at 1.50. Where should your stop-loss sit relative to your entry?
options: It doesn't matter, as long as you have one
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a long position profits when price rises, so the stop-loss sits below, where a fall would prove the trade against you.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — think about which direction actually hurts a long position, and place the stop on that side.

quiz.question: True or False: in a short position, your stop-loss is placed below your entry price.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a short position profits when price falls, so the stop-loss sits above the entry, since a rise is what proves a short position wrong.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — a short profits on a fall, so ask which direction would hurt it. That's where the stop goes.

lessons.title: Inflation — What It Is, and How It Moves Every Market
lessons.keyIdea: Inflation doesn't affect every market the same way — and it doesn't even affect any one market the same way every time.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 established that fiat currency has value purely because people trust it — and that trust can erode. Inflation is what that erosion looks like when you measure it.
A general, sustained rise in the prices of goods and services across an economy, which reduces how much each unit of currency can buy.
Inflation from demand growing faster than the economy's ability to supply goods and services.
Inflation from rising production costs being passed on to consumers.

Most central banks target around 2% inflation, not 0%. Zero inflation removes a central bank's room to maneuver — it can't cut rates to fight a slowdown without risking deflation, which discourages spending and can deepen a recession. Moderate, steady inflation is the target precisely because both extremes are worse.
Forex: central banks fight high inflation by raising interest rates, which tends to attract foreign capital and strengthen a currency.

In late 2021, U.S. inflation ran notably higher than Eurozone inflation. The textbook expectation was a weaker dollar. Instead, the dollar traded near a 16-month high against the euro — fears of renewed European COVID lockdowns outweighed the inflation differential. The relationship wasn't wrong; it was overridden.

Stocks: in the long run, companies can often pass rising costs to consumers. In the short run, rising inflation often pushes stock prices down — a stock's value partly discounts future earnings, and higher inflation increases that discount rate, shrinking the present value of those future profits. Growth stocks, leaning more on distant future earnings, tend to suffer more than value stocks.

Crypto: Bitcoin is often called "digital gold" because its supply is capped at 21 million coins. But short-term price volatility has repeatedly overshadowed that case — an asset that can swing 10% in a day doesn't behave like a stable inflation hedge. Rising rates (the usual inflation response) also tend to pull speculative capital out of crypto, often pushing prices down exactly when the "digital gold" narrative would predict a rise.

lessons.title: Diversification — Why "Don't Put All Your Eggs in One Basket" Is Testable
lessons.keyIdea: Diversification isn't about quantity — owning twenty things isn't automatically safer than owning five. It's about relationship.

blocks.text: Spreading exposure across different assets, sectors, regions, or markets so that a single holding's poor performance doesn't dominate your overall result.
A measure of how closely two assets' prices tend to move in relation to each other, ranging from perfectly together (+1) to perfectly opposite (-1), with 0 meaning no consistent relationship.

A portfolio split evenly across ten tech stocks looks diversified by holding count — but if all ten tend to rise and fall together, it behaves like one large bet, not ten independent ones. This is naive diversification: mistaking the number of holdings for actual risk reduction.
Three words people use interchangeably, and shouldn't:
An asset with an average positive — but imperfect — correlation to your existing holdings. Still tends to move with the rest of your portfolio, just not in lockstep.
An asset with an average correlation at or below zero to another asset, across all conditions — calm markets and turbulent ones alike.
An asset that specifically holds zero or negative correlation during periods of market stress — even if it behaves completely differently the rest of the time.

Two academic studies looked at whether Bitcoin is a safe haven for stock portfolios. One (Journal of Central Banking Theory and Practice, 2026) found Bitcoin showed statistically significant negative correlation with the S&P 500 — a real candidate for safe-haven status. Another found Bitcoin's correlation with stocks rose from roughly 0.05 in 2017 to 0.25–0.30 by 2021, and concluded crypto behaves as a diversifier, not a safe haven. Both studies used real data and careful methods. They still disagree — a sign the underlying relationship genuinely shifts over time.

blocks.text: Diversification reduces risk. It does not remove it. During a genuine broad market shock, correlations across many assets tend to rise together — the calm-market relationships you diversified around can break down exactly when you need them most.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between a "diversifier" and a "safe haven"?
options: A diversifier has an average positive (but imperfect) correlation; a safe haven specifically holds zero/negative correlation during market stress
A safe haven is always gold
A diversifier only applies to forex
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — these are precise, different relationships. An asset can be one without being the other.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — re-read both definitions carefully; they describe different correlation behaviors under different conditions.

quiz.question: True or False: owning a large number of different assets automatically means a portfolio is well-diversified.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — this is the naive diversification trap. Highly correlated holdings can behave like one concentrated bet, no matter how many there are.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — think about ten tech stocks that all move together. Does the count alone protect you?

lessons.keyIdea: Support and resistance are not hard physical barriers — they're levels where enough traders have historically reacted that the reaction becomes somewhat self-reinforcing.

blocks.text: Support and resistance are not hard physical barriers. They can, and do, eventually break. Treat them as a probability, not a guarantee.
Reading the real-time sequence of trade prices, sizes, and volume — originally from a literal paper ticker tape — to gauge buying and selling pressure as it happens.

Jesse Livermore built his reputation on tape reading, starting as a teenager reading ticker tape in the 1890s. His core idea: the tape records actual transactions, not opinions — and actual transactions reflect real buying and selling pressure in a way a chart, updated only after the fact, cannot. Ticker tape disappeared decades ago, replaced by Level II data and order-flow software — but the underlying idea survives in those modern tools.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a bar chart and a candlestick chart?
options: They show the same open/high/low/close data, but candlesticks add a colored body for faster visual reading
Bar charts are only used in forex
Candlestick charts don't show the closing price
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — both show the same four data points per period; candlesticks just make the open/close relationship easier to scan visually.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — both chart types plot identical underlying data. The difference is purely visual presentation.

quiz.question: True or False: a support level is a hard price floor that a price cannot fall below.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — support is a level where price has repeatedly reversed in the past, a historical pattern and probability, not a physical barrier. Support levels break all the time.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — support reflects historical buyer behavior, not a guarantee. It can and does break.

lessons.title: Does It Actually Work? Evidence, Skepticism, and Making a Decision
lessons.keyIdea: A perfect read of a chart, paired with no risk management, is still a losing strategy waiting to happen.

blocks.text: Search any chart pattern's "success rate" and you'll find numbers like "70% for head-and-shoulders" or "88% for a double bottom." These trace back overwhelmingly to one source: Thomas Bulkowski, a private investor who published his own backtested statistics in books and on a personal website — not peer-reviewed, not independently replicated, and by his own data, not stable across time (failure rates nearly doubled between the bullish 1990s and the more volatile 2000s).

While researching this lesson, a live search turned up a trading blog claiming "a study covering over 8,000 chart setups" found a "62% average success rate" — no named author, no journal, no link. Before trusting a number like this, what would you want to see before believing it?
A process where independent experts evaluate a study's methodology and findings before publication, specifically to catch errors or unsupported conclusions.

Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000), published in The Journal of Finance, built an automated, objective system to detect chart patterns and tested it on decades of U.S. stock data. They found several patterns, including head-and-shoulders and double bottoms, provided statistically significant information beyond random chance — but added an important caveat: statistical detectability is not the same as profitability after real-world costs.

Chang & Osler (1999), published in The Economic Journal, tested head-and-shoulders specifically on foreign exchange rates. It did generate statistically significant profits — but was "dominated" by simpler trading rules, meaning a plainer strategy achieved the same or better result with less complexity.

Ghanem, Harasheh, Sbaih & Ajmal (2024), published in Cogent Business & Management — genuinely recent research — tested 497 technical trading rules across 10 currencies over 22 years (2000–2022). Technical trading rules significantly predicted price movements in both developed and emerging-market currencies, with emerging markets showing even higher predictability.

blocks.text: Before trusting any stated success rate: Is this from a peer-reviewed journal, or a personal website/book? Can you find the original source, or only secondhand mentions? Does it specify the market, time period, and conditions tested? Does the number stay consistent across sources, or does it quietly shift?

This closes the loop on everything Foundations has covered. A chart, a candlestick pattern, a support level — all of it is information. None of it is a decision by itself. Risk management is what turns information into a controlled decision. A perfect read of a chart, paired with no risk management, is still a losing strategy waiting to happen. A mediocre read, paired with real risk management, can still be around to trade another day.

quiz.question: What did Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000) actually conclude about chart patterns?
options: Chart patterns guarantee profitable trades 70% of the time
Several patterns provided statistically significant information, but that doesn't automatically mean they're profitable to trade after costs
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — this is the precise, nuanced finding: real signal, not a guarantee of profit.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — re-read the example. The actual finding is more careful than a flat "yes" or "no."

quiz.question: True or False: a statistic repeated across many trading websites is more likely to be accurate because so many sources agree on it.
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — widely repeated statistics often trace back to one non-peer-reviewed original source, just copied and re-copied. Repetition is not independent verification.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite — think about the Bulkowski example. Repetition across blogs doesn't mean independent verification happened.
